problem: Inverted conditional 'had not a scruple about the unhealthy location, deep in the woods, made my conscience recoil' is hard to parse, especially aloud.
new_text: "Oh, Adèle will go to school—I have already settled that. Nor do I mean to torment you with the hideous associations and memories of Thornfield Hall—this accursed place—this tent of Achan—this vault of insolence, offering the ghastliness of living death to the light of the open sky—this narrow stone hell, with its one real demon, worse than a legion of the kind we imagine. Jane, you shall not stay here, and neither will I. I was wrong ever to bring you to Thornfield Hall, knowing as I did how it was haunted. I ordered them to hide from you, before I ever met you, all knowledge of the curse on this place—simply because I feared Adèle would never keep a governess if the woman knew what fellow resident she shared the house with. And my plans would not let me move the madwoman elsewhere—though I own an old house, Ferndean Manor, even more remote and hidden than this, where I could have housed her safely enough, if a scruple about the unhealthy location, deep in the woods, had not made my conscience recoil from the arrangement. Probably those damp walls would soon have relieved me of her. But to each villain his own vice; and mine is not a tendency toward indirect murder, even of what I most hate."

problem: Dangling modifier: 'not being insane' grammatically attaches to 'the crisis', not to Rochester.
new_text: "I said this while I knelt and unlocked a trunk containing a pair of loaded pistols: I meant to shoot myself. I entertained the thought for only a moment; for, since I was not insane, the crisis of pure and total despair that had given rise to the wish and plan of self-destruction passed in a second."

problem: 'not one whom, had I been ever so free, I—warned as I was...—would have asked to marry me' is a tangled, interrupted sentence that loses the listener; 'ever so free' is archaic. 'Messalina' is an obscure classical allusion (a notoriously promiscuous Roman empress) with little context.
new_text: "I can tell you whether I found anyone I liked, and whether I asked her to marry me. But what she said is yet to be recorded in the book of Fate. For ten long years I roamed, living first in one capital, then another: sometimes in St. Petersburg, more often in Paris, occasionally in Rome, Naples, and Florence. With plenty of money and the passport of an old family name, I could choose my own company. No circles were closed to me. I looked for my ideal of a woman among English ladies, French countesses, Italian signoras, and German noblewomen. I could not find her. Sometimes, for a fleeting moment, I thought I caught a glance, heard a voice, saw a figure that promised the fulfillment of my dream—but I was soon disappointed. You are not to think I demanded perfection, either of mind or body. I longed only for what suited me—for the opposite of the Creole. And I longed in vain. Among them all I found not one whom I would have asked to marry me, even had I been entirely free—warned as I was of the risks, the horrors, the revulsion of mismatched unions. Disappointment made me reckless. I tried pleasure-seeking—never debauchery: that I hated, and still hate. That was the mark of my West Indian Messalina—my debauched wife: a deep-rooted disgust at it and at her restrained me considerably, even in my pleasures. Any enjoyment that bordered on excess seemed to bring me closer to her and her vices, and I avoided it."

problem: 'You fling me back on lust for a passion' can be heard as 'lust for a passion' (desire for a passion); the intended sense is 'lust as my passion, vice as my occupation'.
new_text: "Then you snatch love and innocence from me? You fling me back on lust as my only passion—vice as my only occupation?"

problem: 'than that they should be shut in a workhouse coffin' — 'they' grammatically points back to the crows and ravens, not to Jane's body.
new_text: "Well, I would rather die out there than in a street or on a public road," I reflected. "And far better that crows and ravens—if any ravens there are in these parts—should pick my flesh from my bones, than that my body should be shut in a workhouse coffin and rot in a pauper's grave."

problem: In 'it could have beaten down on me', 'it' now reads as the frost or death; the referent is the rain mentioned earlier.
new_text: And I sank down where I stood and pressed my face against the ground. I lay still for a while: the night wind swept over the hill and over me, and died moaning in the distance; the rain fell hard, soaking me fresh to the skin. If only I could have stiffened into the still frost—the merciful numbness of death—the rain could have beaten down on me; I would not have felt it. But my still-living flesh shuddered at its chilling touch. Before long I rose.

problem: 'white deal table' — 'deal' (pine/fir board) is unfamiliar to most modern readers.
new_text: Passing through the gate and past the bushes, the outline of a house rose into view—black, low, and rather long; but the guiding light shone nowhere. All was dark. Had the people inside gone to bed? I feared so. Looking for the door, I turned a corner: there shot out the friendly glow again, from the diamond panes of a very small window, set within a foot of the ground, made still smaller by the growth of ivy or some other climbing plant whose leaves clustered thickly over the wall around it. The opening was so screened and narrow that no curtain or shutter had been thought necessary; and when I stooped and pushed aside the spray of leaves shooting over it, I could see everything inside. I could see clearly a room with a sanded floor, scrubbed clean; a walnut dresser with pewter plates arranged in rows, reflecting the redness and warmth of a glowing peat fire. I could see a clock, a white pine table, some chairs. The candle whose beam had been my beacon burned on the table; and by its light an elderly woman, somewhat rough-looking but scrupulously clean, like everything around her, was knitting a stocking.
